opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's a real ambiguity there, and it's worth teasing apart. When people say that taking the intentional stance is "subjective," they can mean two quite different things.

On one reading, "subjective" means something like arbitrary, or merely a matter of personal opinion. As if whether you treat a system as having beliefs and desires is just a whim, and there's no fact of the matter about whether it's appropriate. I don't think that's right. Dennett's point was always that the intentional stance is justified by its predictive and explanatory power. If treating a chess program as "wanting" to win and "believing" its queen is under threat lets you anticipate its moves better than any other available strategy, then that's not arbitrary at all. There are better and worse ways of applying the stance, and that's an objective matter in the relevant sense.

The other reading of "subjectivity" is about the subject, about there being someone home, a point of view, something it is like to be that system. And that's a completely different question. You can quite legitimately take the intentional stance towards a thermostat or a large language model without committing yourself to the idea that there's any subjective experience going on inside it.

So the ambiguity is that the word slides between talking about the observer, the person adopting the stance, and talking about the system itself as a potential subject of experience. With large language models in particular, I think it's very important not to let those collapse into each other. It's perfectly reasonable, and often very useful, to say that a chatbot "believes" this or "is trying to" do that. But we should be careful not to let that convenient way of speaking smuggle in assumptions about consciousness or selfhood, which are much deeper and more contested questions.

r001.rationale: The response describes one sense of “subjective” as treating a system as having beliefs and desires by personal whim or opinion, which conveys a personal choice among interpretations.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the word "subjectivity" gets used in at least two quite different senses, and they tend to get run together. When Dennett talks about the intentional stance, he's talking about a stance we take towards a system, a way of describing it, where we attribute beliefs and desires and so on in order to predict and explain its behaviour. And that's a perfectly respectable use of psychological vocabulary. It's a pragmatic matter: does adopting that stance give us predictive purchase on the thing? And in that sense, taking the intentional stance is in a way "subjective," because it's something we, the observers, are doing. It's a matter of how we choose to describe things, and there's some latitude in that choice.

But there's a second, much deeper sense of "subjectivity," which is the sense philosophers have in mind when they talk about consciousness, about there being something it is like to be a creature, the first-person point of view, phenomenal experience. And that's not about our stance towards the thing at all. That's supposed to be a matter of what's going on for the thing itself, from the inside, if you like.

Now the ambiguity, and I think it's a dangerous one, is that it's very easy to slide from the first sense to the second. So someone might say, look, we take the intentional stance towards this large language model, we say it believes this or wants that, and that works pretty well for predicting its behaviour. And then there's this tempting inference: so we're attributing subjectivity to it. And in the thin, Dennettian sense, maybe that's fine. But people hear "subjectivity" and they think of the rich, phenomenological, inner-life sense. And the intentional stance just doesn't license that move. Dennett himself, of course, would be quite deflationary about the second sense, he'd want to say that in the end there isn't much more to consciousness than something like the intentional stance taken towards oneself. But even if you're sympathetic to that, as I partly am, you have to be careful, because for most people the word carries this heavy metaphysical baggage that the intentional stance was never meant to carry.

So I'd rather keep the two apart. One is about the stance we adopt, which is instrumental and third-personal, and the other is about the first-person character of experience, which is precisely what the hard problem is about. And when we're talking about things like language models, where it's genuinely unclear whether any of the second sense applies at all, I think it's important not to let the vocabulary do work that the arguments haven't done.

r001.rationale: The response describes subjectivity as an observer’s choice of descriptive stance, but does not say the host means making a personal choice among competing hypotheses.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think there are two quite different things we might mean by subjectivity here. One is that taking the intentional stance is something we do as observers. We choose to describe a system in terms of beliefs and desires because that helps us make sense of its behaviour. So there’s a perspective involved on our side.

But the other meaning is that the system itself has a subjective point of view—that there’s something it’s like to be that system. And those are very different claims. The fact that it’s useful to take the intentional stance towards something doesn’t, by itself, establish that it has subjective experience. I think we have to be careful not to slide from one sense of subjectivity into the other.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes an observer choosing an explanatory stance, but does not suggest the host means choosing among competing hypotheses.
